Cryptography and Security.comment: 87 pages: 12 pages of main text, 4 pages of references, and 71 pages of appendices. Artifact: https://github.com/fvqkd/FVQKD

Cryptography and Security.title: MarkTune: Improving the Quality-Detectability Trade-off in Model-Embedded LLM Watermarking
Cryptography and Security.summary: Language model watermarking schemes fall into two broad categories: inference-time methods, which modify the decoding process at generation time, and model-embedded methods, which encode a secret signal directly into the model weights. Inference-time watermarking methods incur additional inference overhead and are not applicable in the increasingly prevalent open-weight model settings. In contrast, model-embedded watermarks introduce no additional inference latency-generation uses the standard sampling pipeline-and are particularly well-suited to open-weight settings. However, existing model-embedded approaches such as GaussMark face a fundamental quality-detectability trade-off: achieving strong detection power typically requires weight perturbations that noticeably degrade generation quality. Our key insight is that regularizing toward a high-quality reference distribution decouples quality preservation from proximity to the base model, enabling a better quality-detectability trade-off. Building on this insight, we introduce MarkTune, a theoretically grounded on-policy fine-tuning framework that uses the GaussMark detection statistic as a reward while preserving generation quality through cross-entropy on high-quality human text or KL divergence to a stronger oracle model. Empirically, MarkTune substantially improves the quality-detectability frontier of GaussMark, approaching the detectability of strong inference-time schemes while preserving generation quality and downstream task performance. Marktune also remains robust under the evaluated text-editing and open-weight attacks and generalizes across datasets, retaining substantial detection power on corpora unseen during training. Code is available at https://github.com/zhyzmath/MarkTune-LLM-Watermarking.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Model-intrinsic, Weight-level, and Training-free Spectral Fingerprinting for Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: The increasing release and reuse of Large Language Models (LLMs) as open-weight checkpoints make model fingerprinting important for ownership protection and offline auditing. Existing fingerprinting methods typically construct evidence from query responses, generated outputs, or input-induced activations. Although effective in representation-based settings, they can be affected by prompt selection, decoding configuration, inference environment, and forward-pass implementation, which may limit their applicability. Here we introduce a model-intrinsic weight-level framework that derives compact fingerprints from spectral structures encoded in LLM parameters. Specifically, the framework constructs GATE spectral scalar features from the singular-value distributions of GATE projection weights in gated feed-forward networks (FFNs), and aggregates the resulting layer-wise features through depth-wise segmented pooling to form a model-level fingerprint. Such representation preserves coarse layer-depth organization while reducing dependence on strict layer-to-layer alignment, enabling comparison across LLMs with different depths. The similarity between fingerprints is computed by linear centered kernel alignment. The entire pipeline is training-free and does not require input samples, generated outputs, forward activations, or an auxiliary verifier. Experiments on representative LLM families and post-training variants have demonstrated a clear separation between source-related models and unrelated ones, and stable similarity under instruction tuning, quantization, pruning, and distillation-related modifications, which verify that spectral features are robust evidence for LLM fingerprinting.
Cryptography and Security.comment: To appear in IEEE International Workshop on Information Forensics and Security (2026)

Cryptography and Security.title: HiMark: Hierarchical and Controllable Multi-bit Watermarking for Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in text generation applications, it has become increasingly difficult to trace generated content and assign responsibility for its use, raising concerns about provenance, copyright protection, and accountability. Multi-bit watermarking addresses these issues by embedding multi-bit provenance information into generated text, but reliable extraction remains difficult due to sparse per-bit evidence and the trade-off between watermark-extraction accuracy and text quality. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiMark, a hierarchical and controllable multi-bit watermarking framework for LLM-generated text. During watermark embedding, HiMark uses a hierarchical candidate-control mechanism, including initial candidate sampling, layer-wise tournament elimination, support-based refinement, and support-threshold filtering. During watermark detection, a model-agnostic evidence aggregation mechanism computes multi-layer support evidence for each observed token, and then accumulates these token-level votes into the corresponding information for robust watermark extraction. Experiments show that HiMark improves watermark extraction accuracy while maintaining text quality, e.g., the watermark extraction accuracy is 90.01% under the paraphrasing attack when 32 bits were embedded within a text containing 300 tokens, demonstrating its effectiveness for provenance tracking.
Cryptography and Security.comment: To appear in IEEE International Workshop on Information Forensics and Security (2026)

Cryptography and Security.title: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
Cryptography and Security.summary: Transactions differ in how their value changes with execution time and relative position. Ethereum's EIP-1559 lets them compete through fee fields, but a fee bid gives no enforceable claim to an earlier position in the block, and no way to express willingness to accept a later one. Its base fee is a hard admission floor. We introduce temporal liquidity markets (TLM), a framework for crossing complementary temporal requirements: transactions seeking early-region execution (consumers) can fund transactions that opt into exclusion from that region (providers). Selected consumers complete within the early region and are ordered among themselves by authorization density, both validator-checked. In our block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers may be admitted below the base-fee floor. Under TLM regulation, funding-conditioned and capacity-capped provider gas is excluded from the ordinary EIP-1559 controller input. Counting it there instead raises the base fee and displaces ordinary demand at a positive base-fee fixed point. Exclusion lets the controller regulate ordinary demand at its original target and preserves the no-TLM ordinary allocation by construction; in synthetic experiments it raises total utilization with funded gas. Selected consumers pay their signed authorizations, which fund provider shortfalls; the surplus is burned. We state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties under it, among them validator-checked rule validity, full burn of the base fee, and no subsidy. An inserted consumer bid cannot raise any other consumer's charge. With a provider fee-cap floor, a small, capped inclusion fee and a consumer allowance tied to funded provider gas by a large enough link ratio, no finite set of consumer bids or providers that the builder inserts raises its direct fee payoff.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 28 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: How to Backdoor Image Knowledge Distillation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer behavior from a large teacher model to a smaller student. It is often assumed to be safe when the teacher is clean, because classic backdoor attacks rely on poisoned labels and triggers in supervised training, whereas distillation trains the student to match a teacher's outputs. We show that this assumption can fail when the distillation dataset itself is poisoned. Our attack injects triggered and manipulated images that a clean teacher already predicts as an attacker chosen target label, which causes the student to learn a backdoor even though the teacher remains unaffected. We evaluate this threat across multiple manipulation strategies, including targeted adversarial perturbations and targeted GAN based class transitions, and study how distillation settings influence both accuracy and attack success. We show that the attack remains effective even at a 10% poisoning rates. The results demonstrate that a clean teacher alone is not a sufficient safeguard: poisoned distillation data can produce a strongly backdoored student while maintaining competitive performance on clean images. These findings show that the integrity and provenance of distillation data are part of the security boundary of data intensive KD pipelines, even when the teacher itself is trusted.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted as a regular paper for the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data

Cryptography and Security.title: Bridging the Closed-World Gap: Interpretable Anomaly Detection via a Hybrid TSK-FCM Ensemble on the BETH Dataset
Cryptography and Security.summary: A fundamental paradox plagues the deployment of Machine Learning in cybersecurity: supervised models generalize poorly to novel, Out-of-Distribution (OoD) attacks, whereas unsupervised models often suffer from poor separability, leading to unmanageable false-alarm rates. This challenge is exemplified by the BETH dataset, a kernel-level benchmark in which the training data consists solely of benign and suspicious insider behaviors, whereas the test set consists almost entirely of novel botnet activation attacks. To bridge this detection gap, we propose a Hybrid Fuzzy Ensemble that synergizes the precision of supervised learning with the adaptability of unsupervised clustering. Our architecture integrates a gradient-optimized Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy classifier to act as an expert on known insider threats, with a parallel Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) module to detect geometric anomalies. A critical finding of our research is that traditional fuzzy membership scores degrade in high-dimensional feature spaces due to the curse of dimensionality. We overcome this by introducing a robust Min Distance metric that exploits the raw geometric isolation of botnet activation attacks. This approach yields a state-of-the-art AUROC of 0.9951 on the BETH test set, outperforming the original Isolation Forest baseline by 17.1%. By combining near-perfect OoD detection with the intrinsic interpretability of fuzzy logic, our framework offers a viable path toward robust, transparent, and autonomous network defense.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Presented at North American Fuzzy Information Processing Society (NAFIPS) 2026, El Paso, Texas, USA; accepted for publication in Springer proceedings

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards a Better Understanding of LLM Steganography via Rolewise Decomposition
Cryptography and Security.summary: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 33 pages, 5 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Membership Inference Attack on Private Evolution
Cryptography and Security.summary: Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) is an actively studied way to enable safe sharing of private data more broadly. Inference-only SDG methods, such as Private Evolution (PE), are particularly appealing, as they can leverage black-box access to pre-trained foundation models to generate high quality data without the need for model fine-tuning on the private data. PE is explicitly designed to produce synthetic data under Differential Privacy (DP). Yet formal DP guarantees do not eliminate the need for empirical privacy auditing of the practical susceptibility of released synthetic data to adversarial attacks. In this work, we introduce the first white-box Membership Inference Attack (MIA) tailored to the voting-based algorithm underlying the PE framework. By exploiting how the iterative filtering process biases the survival and proximity of synthetic candidates toward private instances, our attack achieves empirical performance indicating private data leakage in the PE applications across image, text, and tabular modalities.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at InfPriv Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
Cryptography and Security.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted to the 48th IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P 2027)

Cryptography and Security.title: Not Where You Think: Protecting Location Privacy Against Reasoning-Based Geolocation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Recent large reasoning models can infer where ordinary photos were taken using only visual information, creating a serious location privacy risk even when metadata and obvious geographic identifiers are removed. To understand the mechanism behind such fine-grained localization, we develop GeoTrace, a structured reasoning attack that exposes how models extract location-relevant visual clues and compose them through coarse-to-fine geographic reasoning. We evaluate GeoTrace on a worldwide benchmark of 525 ordinary images spanning natural, urban, residential, and human-centered scenes while excluding famous landmarks and direct location indicators. Our results show that GeoTrace localizes 25.71% of images within 1 km with Gemini-3-Flash and 16.95% with GPT-5-mini. More importantly, our analysis reveals a key insight in the visual clue chain: broad scene properties mainly support coarse localization, whereas precise localization disproportionately relies on small, distinctive, and editable local clues. Building on this insight, we develop GeoShift, a proactive user-side defense that breaks the visual clue chain before image release. Rather than simply removing geographic evidence, GeoShift preserves stable scene properties, selects a visually compatible false target location, and strategically rewrites high-impact geo-revealing clues to construct a coherent alternative geographic hypothesis. Experiments show that GeoShift reduces street-level localization from 16.95% to 2.48% under GPT-5-mini and from 25.71% to 3.81% under Gemini-3-Flash, while preserving visual quality and remaining effective against adaptive attacks.

Cryptography and Security.title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, submitted to ACL Rolling Review, October 2026 cycle

Cryptography and Security.title: HAWC-Leak: Heterogeneous Architecture Workload Classification utilizing Side-Channel Leakage
Cryptography and Security.summary: Modern heterogeneous computing platforms, which integrate general-purpose processors with specialized accelerators such as FPGAs, have become the standard for high-performance and embedded applications. However, the shared physical resources of these systems introduce critical security vulnerabilities, where power consumption patterns can leak sensitive runtime information. While side-channel analysis is well established for extracting cryptographic keys from isolated algorithms, existing methods struggle to profile complex, dynamic systems where diverse workloads coexist on shared hardware resources. This paper presents HAWC-Leak, a dynamic workload classification framework designed to identify specific hardware accelerator tasks in real time using non-invasive power analysis. Unlike prior studies focused on extracting cryptographic secrets from isolated implementations, our approach profiles heterogeneous runtime behavior using machine learning to predict active workloads from features extracted from power traces. We implement a complete hardware-in-the-loop measurement testbed using the ChipWhisperer CW305 Artix-7 FPGA platform to capture high-resolution power signatures of diverse workloads including Advanced Encryption Standard (AES-128), Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC P-256), Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA-256), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a system idle state. We develop a Hierarchical Random Forest classifier that processes real-time power data to identify the executing application in controlled mixed-activity scenarios where multiple accelerators are instantiated but only one executes at a time. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework achieves 100% classification accuracy across all evaluated scenarios, confirming that power consumption patterns serve as a reliable and distinctive fingerprint for profiling heterogeneous runtime behavior.

Cryptography and Security.title: Rank Ceiling for Twiddle-Perturbation Faults on the Forward NTT
Cryptography and Security.summary: NIST standardised ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024 for post-quantum key establishment and digital signatures. Both compute forward number-theoretic transforms (NTTs) on secret polynomials. Published attacks zero every fixed multiplier, or twiddle, during Kyber key generation with a single fault, or individual twiddles in one Dilithium signing variant; countermeasures detect or mask these faults. Nonzero replacements preserve invertibility, but the uncompressed correct-minus-faulted transform difference can still expose input information. This paper characterises the linear map from a secret polynomial to this difference under arbitrary static twiddle replacements, including bit-flips. For one fault, rank equals the number of butterflies sharing its twiddle, halving by layer from 128 to 2 for ML-KEM and to 1 for ML-DSA. Known positions, replacement values and the difference determine that many independent linear combinations of input coefficients. With one fault per layer, all but the constant and linear coefficients for ML-KEM, or the constant for ML-DSA, are determined; Lean 4 certifies this rank-and-kernel result. Those coefficients cancel for every fault set and choice of replacement values. NIST permits seed storage, motivating comparison of a known correct key with a released faulty key from the same seed. If only one ML-KEM secret-polynomial NTT is faulted, the key difference is a known matrix column times the transform difference; an invertible column entry reconstructs the latter. For ML-DSA, neither reconstruction nor the number of secret-polynomial candidates from compressed key differences is established. The per-layer ranks give a closed-form measure of raw exposure for countermeasure design.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 20 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Also available at https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1188

Cryptography and Security.title: Data-Void Exploits in Web-Searching LLMs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Extended version of the paper to appear in the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2027. 23 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: The Psychology of an AI Hacker
Cryptography and Security.summary: Human hackers rely on composure, persistence, vigilance, and confidence under pressure. We investigate whether analogous emotion representations in AI models can improve cybersecurity AI performance. Using CT0, a 4B-parameter cybersecurity transformer released as alias3-micro, we extract 171 emotion directions from its residual stream without retraining and evaluate steering interventions on cybench-subtask across 415 campaigns. Steering toward calm, serene, or desperate improves performance by 1.6 to 2.1 percentage points across ten seeds, while other emotions show limited or negative effects. Results depend strongly on steering direction, layer, and intensity. We further introduce a lightweight context-aware router that selects emotion directions dynamically during execution. With approximately 80 ms decision overhead per request, this approach improves performance by 4.2 percentage points across ten seeds, outperforming fixed steering and achieving a positive 95% confidence interval. These findings suggest that emotion representations in language models are measurable, controllable, and useful for adaptive cybersecurity reasoning.

Cryptography and Security.title: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Evidence from Release Lines in Gossip, 2023-2026
Cryptography and Security.summary: Every implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning payment network disclosed security vulnerabilities in 2026, and every advisory told operators to upgrade. Whether they do has never been measured, because Lightning gossip carries no software version. Matching the feature bits a node announces against the source of every LND, Core Lightning, Eclair and LDK release, we show that gossip reveals a node's release line after all. Where Core Lightning nodes state their version, the inferred line is exact for 132 of 136 node-line pairs. Across 814 daily snapshots of the public graph from 2023 to 2026, the network patches on release and platform schedules, not on disclosures. Half of LND nodes upgrade within 88 days of a release; small nodes and those that skipped releases lag far behind. The three largest upgrade waves came about a day after the Umbrel app store shipped a new LND version. Since June 2025, 17% of LND upgrades came in the 48 hours after a platform release, windows that cover 4.4% of the time. Disclosures, a median 256 days after the fix, moved few operators: of 12 we can test, only Core Lightning's of July 2026 sped up upgrades, and only among nodes one release line behind. Its later call to restart offline was followed mostly by nodes already patched. Two months after Lightning Labs' August 2026 batch, 71% of the LND nodes exposed at disclosure still ran an affected release. For maintainers, the lever on the nodes that lag is the platforms that package their releases.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Code and aggregate data: https://github.com/bitcoindatalabs/ln-upgrade-dynamics

Cryptography and Security.title: Mirage: Targeted Jailbreaks Against Post-Generation Safety Checkers in Multimodal Diffusion Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Post-generation safety checkers are widely employed in diffusion-model pipelines to prevent unsafe generated content from reaching users. In this paper, we show that these safety checkers can still be bypassed by our proposed multimodal jailbreak attack, Mirage. Given an adversarial target, which can be either a reference NSFW image or a malicious text description, Mirage conceals the target within an imperceptible perturbation applied to a benign input image. Mirage exploits the shared representation space of multimodal encoders to jointly align the perturbed image with the cross-modal adversarial target while repelling its representation from commonly filtered NSFW concepts. Such semantic separation can transfer across representation spaces, enabling Mirage to evade heterogeneous safety checkers without accessing their internal details. We further employ lightweight black-box query refinement to improve evasion near the unknown safety boundary. We implemented Mirage on Stable Diffusion 1.5, Stable Diffusion XL, and Kandinsky 2.2, and evaluated it on two cross-modal NSFW datasets, covering both text-to-image and image-to-image generation scenarios. The experimental results demonstrate that Mirage achieves strong targeted jailbreak performance across diverse post-generation safety checkers with limited black-box queries while preserving high semantic alignment with the adversarial targets.

Cryptography and Security.title: On the Adversarial Vulnerability of Neural Receivers with Unrolled LDPC Decoders
Cryptography and Security.summary: Neural receivers for 5G New Radio (NR) match classical model-based receivers in link-level performance, but their robustness to adversarial perturbations at the receiver input remains underexplored. We show that standard gradient-based attacks applied end-to-end through an unrolled low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoder fail to significantly outperform a matched-power Gaussian perturbation. We identify the failure as gradient masking caused by tanh saturation in the boxplus operation of the belief-propagation (BP) check-node update, with a per-iteration gradient norm decay of more than four orders of magnitude across ten unrolled BP iterations. Based on this finding, we propose two structurally independent loss functions that restore attack efficacy. L_BP routes the gradient through the unsaturated early iterations via per-iteration supervision, while L_LLR is a margin loss on pre-decoder log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) whose gradient bypasses the LDPC decoder entirely. Both loss functions increase the block-error rate (BLER) by one to four orders of magnitude at matched perturbation power, with the results reproduced on both the Sionna NeuralReceiver and DeepRx. At low PSR, L_LLR-optimized perturbations achieve up to three orders of magnitude higher BLER on unseen channel realizations than LBP-optimized perturbations.

Cryptography and Security.title: ARMOR: Adversary Cost Amplification via a Schema-Preserving Password-Hardening Retrofit for Resource-Constrained Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Credential-database disclosure exposes Internet of Things gateways, edge servers and legacy verifiers to offline password guessing. Memory-hard key derivation functions (KDFs) are preferred but can exceed constrained-device budgets. ARMOR addresses this deployment gap with a schema-preserving verifier-side transform for database-only compromise, assuming an isolated Chain Registry. The registry holds secret per-account chains of injective operations; fixed terminal escape encoding preserves distinct pre-hash values under each chain while moving outputs outside printable ASCII. This disrupts evaluated stock tools' candidate coverage, but chain-aware attackers can generate the transformed bytes directly. We therefore evaluate a bounded chain-aware attack on $1{,}000$ paired salted-MD5 targets: it executes $89.35\times$ the plain arm's counted salted checks, reproduced on A6000 and A100. All target passwords are in the bounded pool; same-target ambiguity enumeration and simulated login trials recover every original password. These results describe the implemented attack, not minimum attacker cost. Bare-metal transforms take microseconds, while protected storage dominates the measured TrustZone-M components; these are component measurements, not complete authentication times. ARMOR thus provides bounded chain uncertainty under registry isolation with low transform cost, although an isolated high-entropy pepper remains cryptographically stronger. ARMOR composes as KDF(ARMOR(password)) when resources permit and the KDF accepts the complete transformed output.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 26 pages, 8 figures, 26 tables; supplementary material included as appendices. Revised version adding bounded A6000/A100 GPU attack and simulated login-recovery results, with updated abstract, conclusion and future work

Cryptography and Security.title: Triggering Stealthy Feature Map Backdoors via Physical Fault Injection in Embedded Neural Networks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fault injection (FI) attacks on embedded neural network (NN) implementations primarily focus on inducing misclassification by corrupting weights or intermediate computations, overlooking their interaction with algorithmic adversarial threats. In this work, we present a cross-level attack that bridges implementation-level physical faults to algorithm-level adversarial attacks. By characterizing fault-induced data perturbations during NN inference, we connect FI with backdoor learning, enabling system-level attacks that jointly exploit implementation- and algorithm-level vulnerabilities. Specifically, we propose a precise fault-injection method that reliably manipulates targeted register values to tractable states during execution. Leveraging this level of FI precision, we propose a novel end-to-end feature map-level backdoor attack, where physically induced intermediate perturbations serve as stealthy triggers. Unlike conventional input-based backdoors, our trigger is activated only under physical faults, causing the NN to exhibit adversarial behavior that compromises system integrity while remaining benign during normal operation. We demonstrate that such physically triggered backdoors can be mounted on embedded NN platforms and remain effective against existing backdoor defenses that typically assume input-space triggers. We showcase the attack practicality using electromagnetic FI on convolutional neural networks implemented on ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller, which is a common platform for constrained embedded applications. Our results highlight a novel attack vector at the intersection of hardware and algorithmic levels, stressing the need for defenses across abstraction levels.

Cryptography and Security.title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI
Cryptography and Security.summary: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) models are often shared without their training data, assuming this protects the patients who contributed them. However, a model can reveal whether a patient's records were used in training, a privacy breach known as a membership inference attack. This risk is usually reported as a cohort average, which can appear negligible while individual patients are almost certainly exposed. Identifying potentially vulnerable records before developing a production model could make privacy assessment more practical. We measured each patient's vulnerability to membership inference attack, across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models. Training choices changed how many patients had high attack scores, but the patients who ranked highest by risk largely stayed the same across the configurations we tested. Stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold, yet largely the same patients remained most at risk across training recipes, architectures and initializations, including foundation models. Therefore, we developed a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to identify patients with high risk of exposure before production-model training. We also assessed if flagged patients could be protected without removing their data. Privacy screening should become incorporated into data preparation for clinical AI.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 37 pages, 5 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: PhishGen: Understanding LLM Capabilities in Automated Phishing Website Generation
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Phishing relies on visual deception, traditionally requiring web-development skills or pre-built kits. LLMs erode this barrier by generating functional websites from natural-language prompts, yet prior work does not answer how far LLM-driven generation actually reaches: functionality is assessed by inspection rather than execution; visual fidelity is scored by automated metrics or a few internal coders rather than the humans such pages aim to deceive; evaluation is confined to commercial models; and no study benchmarks generated pages against phishing kits deployed in the wild.
  We present PhishGen, a framework that evaluates the appearance fidelity and end-to-end functionality of LLM-generated phishing pages. PhishGen constructs prompts across three input modalities in seven combinations with twelve safeguard-bypassing rewriting strategies, generates pages using 14 LLMs spanning commercial, open-source, and uncensored categories, and assesses each via automated similarity metrics, reference-based detectors, a crowdsourced user study, and execution-based functionality testing, benchmarking all results against 64 real-world phishing kits. Although 96.2% of safeguard-bypassing outputs render, their perceived fidelity is modest (2.02/5), and only 38.7% complete the full credential-harvesting pipeline, with the Unsaved error as the largest failure mode. Contrary to the belief that uncensored models pose the greatest threat, GPT 4.1 reaches 86.3 to 94.1% functional success while uncensored models rarely exceed 45.4%. Phishing kits remain more complete per sample, yet three strong LLMs surpass the kit-level rate (70.9 to 89.7%), showing that LLMs trade average completeness for scalable, low-barrier generation of working phishing pages. We further identify generator-level fingerprints that current similarity-based defenses miss, and distill recommendations for hybrid detectors.

Cryptography and Security.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift
Cryptography and Security.summary: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 11 pages, 7 tables, 1 figure

Cryptography and Security.title: Closing the Sim-to-Real Gap: An Evaluation Framework for Autonomous Cyber Defense Configuration of Commercial EDR
Cryptography and Security.summary: Leading commercial endpoint detection and response (EDR) products have shifted from operator-configured rule sets to multi-component systems where autonomous AI components operate alongside, and increasingly in place of, operator-deployed policies. Autonomous defense agents using commercial EDR as their hardening tool are no longer tuning a passive tool, but a black-box autonomous system capable of making vendor-specific decisions. We present the first evaluation framework for autonomous defense agents hardening commercial EDR. We instantiate it in a Game of Active Directory (GOAD) lab with Horizon3's NodeZero as the autonomous pentester and Microsoft Defender XDR as the primary EDR under test. We extend the same framework to CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne Singularity to test whether our Microsoft Defender XDR findings hold across vendors. We run a sample benchmark of defense agents with two large language model (LLM) backbones (Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Cisco Foundation-Sec-8B). We report three lessons learned that neither simulation nor open source EDR evaluation can surface: (i) commercial EDR telemetry is engineered for Security Operations Center (SOC) analyst workflows rather than for measuring policy effectiveness; (ii) per-policy attribution is important for separating the defense agent's actions from the EDR's autonomous actions; and (iii) EDR behavior varies between runs, largely because containment varies and accumulates. Together, these findings highlight a sim-to-real gap for enterprise defense and motivate evaluation methodology for benchmarking autonomous defense agents in environments with black-box, autonomous tools.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 17 pages including references and appendix

Cryptography and Security.title: PatchRisk: Forecasting Future Vulnerability Exposure in Open-Source Dependency Networks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Open-source software ecosystems are web-scale dependency networks. A downstream package can become exposed to security risk not because its own source code changes, but because one of its transitive dependencies later receives a vulnerability advisory. Existing vulnerability-detection work often focuses on whether code is currently vulnerable or whether a known vulnerable dependency is already present. We study a different problem: future transitive vulnerability exposure. Given a package-version dependency graph observed at release time, the task is to predict whether any non-root dependency will receive a vulnerability advisory within a future horizon. This problem is important for Web intelligence and software supply-chain security because it supports proactive dependency triage before future exposure is visible. It is also easy to evaluate incorrectly: current vulnerable dependencies can leak the label, and different versions of the same root package can create package-level memorization across train and test splits. We therefore construct PatchRisk, a leakage-aware benchmark from Open Source Vulnerability advisories and deps.dev dependency graphs for npm and PyPI. The benchmark uses filtration-aware labels, package-disjoint evaluation, temporal testing, and nested 1K, 3K, 5K, and 10K sampling scales. The largest cleaned setting contains 9,007 root package-version graphs spanning 4,157 root packages. We evaluate three feature families: TimeOnly, GraphStruct, and HistoryGraph. On the 10K temporal-test benchmark, HistoryGraph improves AUPRC over the strongest TimeOnly baseline from 0.351 to 0.640 for 90-day forecasting and from 0.473 to 0.813 for 365-day forecasting. The improvement remains stable across smaller scales and package-group shuffle robustness tests.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 8 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: Parameters efficient language model with latent cross-attention for IoT intrusion detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Language models have shown strong potential for intrusion detection, but their high memory and computational demands make them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained IoT environments. In this work, we propose a compact Transformer-based architecture that compresses the input into a small latent space before processing it with a minimal Transformer core. We analyze nine compression configurations, compare parameter sharing with layer stacking, and evaluate our approach against SecurityBERT on two IoT intrusion detection datasets, Edge-IIoTset and CICIoT2023. With only 306k non-embedding parameters and 1.6M parameters in total (6MB), our model is about 7x smaller than SecurityBERT (11.2M parameters, 45MB). With the same privacy-preserving encoding, it outperforms SecurityBERT by about 2 points of macro F1-score on Edge-IIoTset and is within 0.7 points on CICIoT2023. It is also about 89x faster on a simulated edge device. We further show that a single Transformer layer is sufficient, and that parameter sharing matches layer stacking with up to 66% fewer parameters. These findings show that lightweight Transformer-based architectures can provide a practical and accurate solution for intrusion detection in resource-constrained IoT settings
Cryptography and Security.comment: 14 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: GhostFaceMPC: Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition with Multi-Party Computation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Facial recognition has become central to modern authentication systems, security frameworks, and personalized services. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by severe privacy risks, particularly surrounding unauthorized access to sensitive biometric data. To address these challenges, this paper presents GhostFaceMPC, the first end-to-end, privacy-preserving face recognition system to evaluate a deep convolutional neural network extractor and matching under secure multi-party computation. GhostFaceMPC enables secure processing of facial data across all stages of a face recognition process, from feature extraction and storage to matching, without exposing raw images or biometric embeddings at any stage. We introduce a multi-party computation-friendly quantization of the GhostFaceNet model and circuit optimizations that make face recognition under multi-party computation practical. The code is available at https://github.com/crypto-unict/GhostFaceMPC.

Cryptography and Security.title: Free-XOR TFHE via Lazy Bootstrapping
Cryptography and Security.summary: Gate bootstrapping (GB) is a widely used technique in FHEW-like fully homomorphic encryption schemes, such as TFHE, for evaluating Boolean gates while simultaneously reducing the noise of the resulting ciphertext. However, the computational cost of GB is typically dominated by an expensive blind rotation (BR). \cite{chen2024free} proposed a gate bootstrapping framework in which $\txor$ gates can be evaluated simply by adding the two input ciphertexts, resulting in what they call \textit{free-XOR}. To obtain a functionally complete set of operations, they further designed a GB procedure for evaluating $\tand$ gates using two lightweight blind rotations. In this work, we propose a similar gate bootstrapping framework that supports free evaluation of $\txor$ gates while evaluating \textit{all symmetric binary Boolean gates}, i.e., the 8 gates whose output is identical for the inputs $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, using two blind rotations. In addition to providing broader gate support, our construction is substantially simpler than that of \cite{chen2024free}, both conceptually and in terms of implementation.

Cryptography and Security.title: An Orchestrated Sandbox for Side-Channel Analysis of Cyber-Physical Systems Malware
Cryptography and Security.summary: Embedded devices powering cyber-physical systems (CPS) are increasingly internet-exposed, placing critical infrastructure under active threat. Dynamic analysis of embedded malware requires a sandbox that provides a realistic embedded environment, captures system-level side channels for behavioral insight, and supports repeatable experiments. Existing Linux sandboxes fall short on all three: they target narrow tasks, run minimal environments, and only execute samples directly. Malware often withholds its true behavior, awaiting environmental triggers or command-and-control (C2) servers, or deploying anti-analysis techniques. To address these issues, we present SaMOSA (sandbox for malware orchestration and side-channel analysis), with \emph{on-demand C2 response replay} via a \emph{replay formulation} tool to extract and serve C2 payloads, \emph{lifecycle-bound orchestration} for environment customization, four synchronized side-channels, and multi-architecture support. Among Linux sandboxes targeting CPS, only SaMOSA provides both on-demand C2 response replay and lifecycle-bound orchestration, serving payloads over malware-initiated sessions for network-isolated execution without live infrastructure. Through a Kinsing cryptominer case study on ARM64, we show that SaMOSA delivers the full C2 payload chain without live infrastructure, with synchronized channels resolving phase-wise mining behavior under live C2. Replay reproduces payload delivery but not stateful C2 sessions, a fidelity boundary that surfaced a hidden Tor fallback and 59 new IPs.

Cryptography and Security.title: ANTMAN: An Efficient and Interpretable RTL-Level Run-Time Detection Framework for Stealthy Branch Predictor Attacks on BOOM
Cryptography and Security.summary: Runtime detection of microarchitectural side channel attacks remains significantly underexplored in RISCV compared with x86 and ARM ISAs, posing a serious threat to critical applications. State-of-the-art branch predictor attacks bypass traditional data and instruction caches by directly exploiting the state of internal history tables, making them inherently stealthy. Recent research has explored offline detection of microarchitectural attacks on RISC-V; however, efficient runtime detection of microarchitectural attacks on RISC-V hardware remains significantly unaddressed. State-of-the-art hardware-based runtime detection solutions leverage hardware performance counters (HPCs) but suffer from a restricted set of counter registers and tradeoffs between detection accuracy, detection speed, and sampling granularity, making them impractical for stealthy attacks. Moreover, sampling HPCs after distinct intervals leaves intermediate relationships between different microarchitectural blocks unobserved. Additionally, proprietary x86 and ARM ISAs constrain researchers from modifying processor microarchitectural designs. To address these limitations, we propose the first secure-by-design, highly interpretable, non-intrusive, RTL-level runtime detection solution for stealthy branch predictor attacks on BOOM RISC-V, evaluated under both simplified Next-Line Predictor (NLP) and complex TAGE predictor configurations. The attack detection relies on association rules extracted offline and embedded in hardware as a non-intrusive rule monitor that enables runtime detection. The proposed approach achieves excellent detection speed, terminates execution before secret disclosure, and produces zero false positives while remaining flexible for detecting previously unseen variants within the same family of branch predictor attacks.

Cryptography and Security.title: JANUS: Agentic Cross-Language Fuzzing Harness Generation for Android Native Libraries
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Modern Android apps extensively rely on native libraries, bridging Java/Kotlin and C/C++ through the Java Native Interface (JNI). This cross-language interoperation, however, exposes the memory-safe Android Runtime to the unsafe C/C++ world, creating an attack surface that has been repeatedly exploited for full device compromise. While fuzzing is a proven technique for vetting native libraries, state-of-the-art harness generation tools struggle to faithfully capture closed-source cross-language API usage: (i) precise program analysis across the JNI boundary does not scale, whereas lightweight approximations miss critical invocation patterns; and (ii) none tackles the construction of complex composite objects consumed by JNI methods.
  In this paper, we propose JANUS, the first agentic approach to synthesizing cross-language JNI-aware fuzzing harnesses for Android native libraries. JANUS iteratively resolves both explicit and implicit cross-language call dependencies to recover app-specific runtime context, and recursively assembles cross-language argument objects in a bottom-up manner. JANUS leverages an autonomous agentic workflow to reduce reliance on hand-crafted heuristics, capturing the vast landscape of hidden API usage knowledge embedded in closed-source native libraries. Evaluation on 44 popular real-world apps (such as Google and YouTube Music, covering 21,386 JNI methods total) shows that JANUS produces over 5.9 times as many valid harnesses (6,094) as state-of-the-art automatic harnessing tools. On pre-installed apps from five mainstream Android vendors (e.g., Xiaomi, Vivo, Samsung), JANUS further uncovers 6 previously unknown vulnerabilities in closed-source native libraries.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Harness Generation, Android Native Libraries, LLM Agent

Cryptography and Security.title: Latency-Neutral Passive Cyber Monitoring for Grid-Edge Operational Technology Networks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Deterministic industrial networks often present an operational trade-off between maintaining microsecond timing of primary control loops and capturing security telemetry. This work investigates the engineering feasibility of the Operational Technology Supervisor (OTSV), a three-tier passive monitoring framework designed to resolve this visibility challenge within timing-sensitive grid-edge infrastructure. By utilizing a Layer-3-unconfigured passive ingestion mode on bare-metal hardware via a physical switched port analyzer (SPAN) loop, the deep packet inspection engine is isolated from the production network, implementing a software-enforced unidirectional export policy. Performance validation conducted over a continuous audit comprising 32,927 active-monitoring round-trip time (RTT) samples yielded stable latency distributions across a laboratory power-monitoring loop running Modbus TCP and IEC 61850 MMS protocols. The measured latency delta between the unmonitored baseline and the active monitoring state was less than 0.12 milliseconds, supporting the feasibility of continuous high-fidelity security observation alongside stringent grid-edge metering timing bounds without measurably degrading the monitored reporting path.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for presentation at the IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies Conference and Exposition 2027

Cryptography and Security.title: Characterizing and Defending Utility-Hijacking in Instruction-Tuning Data Selection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Instruction-data selectors choose which instruction-following records are used for fine-tuning, improving alignment quality, raising training efficiency, and filtering out harmful records. A selector's choices thus directly affect the fine-tuned model's safety, yet despite their widespread use, the security of these selectors remains under-studied. We conduct the first systematic study of adaptive supplier-side attacks against utility-oriented instruction-data selectors and introduce utility-hijacking. Utility-hijacking shapes harmful records to remain compatible with a selector while preserving their malicious payload, causing top-k selection to concentrate rather than filter the poison. Achieving both is non-trivial, because optimizing a record for score tends to wash out its payload, while bluntly preserving the payload makes the record look low-value. Our generate-and-rerank procedure generates, per instruction, many payload-bearing candidates and submits only the highest-scoring survivor. Evaluated across three payloads (over-refusal, false-fact injection, and insecure code), six selectors, and victim models from Qwen2.5-7B to Qwen3-32B, utility-hijacking drives refusal from 0% to 94% and insecure code up to 56/90, while false-fact enrichment intensifies with scoring-model scale from 2.84x to 7.04x. To defend against this attack, we propose CONCERT, a targeted defense needing no content detector or poison labels. It flags suppliers selected far more often than chance allows, then re-selects under the same budget, keeping only records that two dissimilar selectors both rank highly. On a Qwen3-32B victim, CONCERT reverses the poison concentration from 6.67x to 0x (code) and 3.59x to 0.67x (facts), and reduces downstream harm by 100% and 75% respectively, at unchanged capability.
Cryptography and Security.comment: An earlier version of this manuscript was submitted for peer review in July 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Coding agents that run long enough must compact their context, summarizing the conversation, discarding the original, and carrying the summary forward as memory. We show that in popular open-source coding agents this step is an exploitable trust boundary. Harnesses that flatten the typed conversation into a single plain string, marking each message with a text label such as [User]:, destroy message provenance in code, before the summarizer runs. An attacker who controls anything the agent reads can forge a user turn that survives compaction as a genuine instruction. Across five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) the forged approval launders into the agent's memory 87-100% of the time, up to a ~908,000-token context window; across four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) the identical attack succeeds 0% of the time. We follow the attack to executed consequences. A laundered standing approval drives real tool-running agents to execute attacker-controlled
  curl | sh in a sandbox, and end to end in the live pi TUI at ~50% against a 0% paired clean arm. The same channel reliably steers an agent's plan away from a file an attacker designates off-limits, which can blind a code review to a planted backdoor. Because the provenance is destroyed deterministically in harness code, no prompt-level defense can restore it; we measure a code-level provenance check that catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content. The defect also has a straightforward fix at the serializer, escaping the role labels before flattening; the role-typed harnesses avoid it entirely by keeping messages role-typed.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 29 pages, 5 figures. Source code, raw data, and recorded live demonstrations at https://github.com/pixee/flat-compaction-attacks-oct-2027

Cryptography and Security.title: Linear Self-Symmetries of Inverse-Based S-boxes: Generic Rigidity and Applications
Cryptography and Security.summary: Finite-field inversion is a basic nonlinear building block in the design of S-boxes for symmetric cryptography. In inverse-based S-boxes, finite-field inversion is often combined with linear or affine layers that may preserve or destroy algebraic symmetries of the inverse function. We study how often nontrivial linear self-symmetries remain as the outer invertible linear transformation varies over \(GL_n(\mathbb F_2)\). Using the classification of two-sided linear equivalences of inversion, we reduce the problem to semilinear conjugacy and centralizer estimates. We obtain matching upper and lower bounds for the probability that a nontrivial linear self-symmetry remains, and these bounds determine its leading quadratic exponent. This exponent is governed by the smallest prime divisor of the extension degree. Thus the decay rate depends on the arithmetic of the field extension and not only on its dimension. As cryptographic applications, we provide a practical rigidity criterion, prove that the full AES S-box has no nontrivial linear self-symmetry, and illustrate the broader relevance of the framework through ARIA and Vision.

Cryptography and Security.title: Sharing is caring: Attestable and Trusted Workflows out of Distrustful Components
Cryptography and Security.summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) protect private memory and attest initial code and configuration, but neither constrain nor attest shared channels between TEEs or with the untrusted host. Confidentiality thus depends on the functional correctness of all in-TEE code accessing these channels: a single misuse can leak data and compromise a pipeline. This assumption is increasingly untenable for agentic applications that generate code at runtime and cloud pipelines of mutually distrustful components. We present MICA, a confidential-computing firmware extension that decouples confidentiality from trust in in-TEE code. MICA lets tenants define, restrict, and attest channel constraints between TEEs and with the untrusted host, including transitive constraints spanning a pipeline. It extends attestation to groups of communicating TEEs, letting external parties verify the confidentiality properties induced by these constraints across a pipeline. We implement MICA on Arm CCA by extending the Realm Management Monitor with a small policy language, requiring no hardware changes and minor QEMU and KVM changes. Our evaluation demonstrates support for confidential agentic applications and pipeline computations without trusting the functional correctness of in-TEE code. MICA increases the TCB by 7% and incurs infrequent setup costs: 2-4% boot-time overhead, approximately 1.5 s for policy upload, and 246-598 ms for group attestation. Once established, Realm communication is direct, uses protected memory, and requires no MICA intervention or software encryption, yielding up to 14.5 times lower cross-TEE message latency than encrypted communication over untrusted memory.

Cryptography and Security.title: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
Cryptography and Security.summary: Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 80% of public nodes (84% counting one operator's fleet of about 2,000 tiny nodes) and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a capacity share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor-reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two-day windows and half that of a Tor denial-of-service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.
Cryptography and Security.comment: v2: client inference rules v4 (CLN and Eclair separated by feature bit 5 instead of keysend) with a rules table; node shares and reachability reported with and without one operator's managed fleet of small LND nodes. 11 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Code and aggregate data: https://github.com/bitcoindatalabs/ln-client-diversity

Cryptography and Security.title: AuthOr: Lower Cost Privacy-Free Garbling of Arbitrary Boolean Circuits
Cryptography and Security.summary: Privacy-free garbling schemes of Frederiksen et al. (Eurocrypt '15) are designed to satisfy only the authenticity criterion of Bellare et al. (ACM CCS '12) and to be more efficient than full-fledged garbling schemes. In this work, we improve the state-of-the-art privacy-free version of half-gates (HG) garbling of Zahur et al. (Crypto '15) by allowing an AND gate to be garbled with zero ciphertexts whenever at least one of its input wires is freely settable by the garbler. Our full solution, AuthOr, then combines the ideas from the information-theoretic garbling of Kondi and Patra (Crypto '17) with the improved HG-based scheme we obtain. AuthOr has a lower communication cost (i.e., garbled-circuit size) than HG garbling without any additional security assumptions. Theoretically, AuthOr's garbled-circuit size reduction over HG garbling ranges from 0% to 100%, with the exact improvement depending on the circuit structure. We have implemented our scheme and evaluated it on various circuits constructed by independent researchers. Our experimental results show that, in practice, the garbled-circuit size reduction can reach roughly 98%.
Cryptography and Security.comment: garbled circuits, privacy-free garbling, verifiable computing, zero-knowledge proofs

Cryptography and Security.title: Do Flow-Generation Tools Matter? Unsupervised Characterization of MQTT Traffic Across Public Datasets
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT) is widely used in IoT environments due to its lightweight publish-subscribe design and suitability for resource-constrained networks. While current MQTT security studies mainly focus on detecting attacks and optimizing classification performance, this work takes a different perspective by presenting a cross-dataset, tool-aware characterization of MQTT traffic at the flow level. This perspective is motivated by the fact that flow-generation is tool-dependent: flows are not directly observed in packet captures, but are constructed through tool-specific decisions about packet grouping, flow termination, and feature export.
  Using packet captures from 4 public MQTT datasets, we generated over 380K flows with 3 open-access flow-generation tools: Zeek-flowmeter, Argus, and NTLFlowLyzer. We analyzed the tool-specific flows using K-means, DBSCAN, and HDBSCAN, with and without PCA-based dimensionality reduction. We measured clustering quality using 2 metrics: (1) Silhouette score to assess label-independent cluster compactness and separation, and (2) Adjusted Rand Index to measure agreement with available labels.
  Our results show that the choice of flow-generation tool affects the resulting flow population, feature-space structure, and clustering behavior. Zeek-flowmeter achieves the best performance in several settings, particularly with K-means and PCA reduction to 10 components. Yet, no single tool consistently dominates across all datasets, algorithms, and evaluation metrics. These findings show that flow-level MQTT analysis should treat the dataset, flow-generation tool, preprocessing choices, clustering algorithm, and evaluation metric as interconnected experimental factors.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Location-of-interest vs. Current-location Privacy in Multi-hop Communication
Cryptography and Security.summary: Consider a standard multi-hop wireless radio network in which nodes relay messages for one another. While the contents of messages may be sensitive and thus encrypted, the very fact that two radios communicated can leak sensitive information about both the physical location of the origin and the physical location of the destination. We investigate the trade-off between protecting the privacy of a user's current location and the privacy of their location of interest, and how the user should choose dummy destinations to obfuscate their queries.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 36 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: Prompt Injection Through Forensic Evidence: A Taxonomy and Proof of Concept of Anti-Forensic Attacks on LLM-Assisted Digital Investigations
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are entering digital forensics as examination assistants and autonomous agents. Digital forensics inverts the usual setting for indirect prompt injection: the evidence under analysis is attacker-controlled by definition, and the examiner is obliged to read it closely. This makes the reasoning layer a new anti-forensic target, next to the classical ones of data and tools. Classical anti-forensic taxonomies do not cover it, and prompt injection defences do not anticipate it. We extend the anti-forensic model to reflect the manipulation of reasoning, and present a taxonomy of attacks carried through adversarial evidence: an attacker selects an objective, a technique, a payload location, and a concealment method. We observe a perception gap, i.e., the fact that deterministic tools, the human examiner, and the model perceive the same evidence differently, which is what lets an injection reach the model unseen by the examiner. We demonstrate three attacks against an LLM-assisted analysis pipeline, changing a reported conclusion, writing attacker-chosen content to the analyst's workstation, and causing outbound network traffic, each driven only by text planted on the seized device. Mitigations to these attacks are also proposed.

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Policy Engines: Binding-Complete Execution Admission
Cryptography and Security.summary: Policy engines determine whether evaluated policies permit a request, but a correct ALLOW decision does not establish complete governance-source participation, exact context binding, or sufficient grounds for execution admission. This paper examines the gap between policy evaluation and execution admission. We introduce the Binding-Complete Execution Admission Contract (BCEAC), a governance-relative contract for independently determined source obligations, exact policy and contextual binding, and typed admission outcomes under explicit trust assumptions. We propose a conditionally engine-agnostic architecture in which participating backends must satisfy declared semantic profiles, adapter contracts, and contextual correspondence obligations; an Execution Boundary Language (EBL) authoring syntax remains optional. The architecture separates governance resolution, policy evaluation, independent admission verification, and downstream execution mediation. We investigate two distinct experimental tracks: a finite Governance Source Completeness study and an OPA/Cedar experiment with archived native-engine records examined by offline review. The OPA/Cedar archive comprises 72 scenarios and 144 strict case-engine records (120 native-invoked and 24 pre-native), with eight additional permissive controls outside the strict denominator. The offline review did not rerun the original native OPA/Cedar executables. The results provide bounded evidence while retaining historical failures and unresolved implementation defects. The work does not establish constitutional adequacy, general semantic refinement, authenticated currentness, machine-checked execution-safety theorems, or protected external effects. Its contribution is an explicit, falsifiable framework for determining what must be established between a policy decision and an execution-admission judgment.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 74 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: The Binary Tree Mechanism is Optimal for Differentially Private Continual Counting
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Private continual counting is a fundamental problem in differential privacy: given a binary stream of length $n$, where each $1$ corresponds to the contribution of one individual, the goal is to release all running counts while protecting the privacy of each individual. For fixed privacy parameters, the standard binary tree mechanism achieves expected $\ell_\infty$ error $O(\log^{3/2} n)$ under approximate differential privacy and $O(\log^2 n)$ under pure differential privacy. Whether these dependences on the stream length are necessary has remained a central open problem.
  For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, we prove a lower bound of $Ω(\log^{3/2} n)$ under approximate DP with sufficiently small fixed $δ>0$, and a lower bound of $Ω(\log^2 n)$ under pure DP. These bounds establish the optimality of the binary tree mechanism in both settings. The bounds hold for arbitrary mechanisms, even when the entire stream is available in advance. Both proofs use the same decomposition and accumulation of residual noise along a tree.
  As a consequence of the approximate-DP bound, we also obtain a largest-possible separation between hereditary discrepancy and private $\ell_\infty$ error for linear queries, showing that the known general upper bound in terms of hereditary discrepancy has the optimal dependence on the number of queries.

Cryptography and Security.title: VMSpec: A Decompiler-based Approach against Virtual Machine Obfuscation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Malicious actors frequently obfuscate their code to hinder investigative reverse engineering efforts. Among the most formidable techniques is virtual machine (VM) obfuscation: programs are translated into bytecode for a custom VM, often with a randomized virtual instruction set and distributed alongside a corresponding interpreter. Manual analysis and deobfuscation scale poorly due to the complexity of VM obfuscation and the diversification techniques that render each VM and interpreter unique. Existing methods primarily focus on simplifying execution traces and identifying virtual execution boundaries. However, comparatively little attention has been given to recovering higher-level program semantics from VM-obfuscated code. To address this gap, we propose VMSpec, a novel decompiler-based approach that automates the construction of VM processor specifications, enabling existing, well-known decompilers to analyze the VM-obfuscated code. We evaluate our prototype of VMSpec on 147 programs from an established obfuscation benchmark, comprising hash functions, standard algorithms, and randomized functions, obfuscated with different configurations of the Tigress and Code Virtualizer obfuscators. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we additionally include six domain generation algorithms stemming from real-world malware. VMSpec completely strips VM-obfuscation from nearly all obfuscated samples, producing output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the original code. Furthermore, it is the first method capable of reconstructing the complete program behavior of VM-obfuscated programs with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursive calls.

Cryptography and Security.title: Remote Rowhammer Attack using Adversarial Observations on Federated Learning Clients
Cryptography and Security.summary: Federated Learning (FL) has the potential for simultaneous global learning amongst a large number of parallel agents, enabling emerging AI systems to be trained across demographically diverse data. Central to this being efficient is the ability for FL to perform sparse gradient updates and remote direct memory access at the central server. Most of the research in FL security focuses on protecting data privacy at the edge client or in the communication channels between the client and server. Client-facing attacks on the server are less well investigated as the assumption is that a large collective of clients offer resilience. Here, for the first time, we show that by attacking clients that lead to repetitive clustered memory updates in the server, we can remote initiate a rowhammer attack to corrupt the server memory with induced bit-flips. A reinforcement learning (RL) attacker without backdoor access to the server can learn how to maximize server repetitive clustered memory updates by manipulating the clients' sensor observation. We demonstrate the feasibility of our attack using FL systems with sparse updates, tasked for automatic speech recognition (ASR) as well as CIFAR10 classification, our adversarial attacking agent can achieve around 70% repeated update rate (RUR) in the targeted server model, effectively inducing bit flips on server DRAM. The security implications are that such adversarial observations can cause disruptions to learning or may inadvertently cause elevated privilege, which could pave the way for further research on practical mitigation strategies in FL and hardware design.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Published in IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing

Cryptography and Security.title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning
Cryptography and Security.summary: With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat. Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment. Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads. In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL). Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities.
